content: Chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus) has specific dosing recommendations based on the condition being treated. For general use, the recommended oral dose is 6-3 mg taken twice daily (BID) or 35-45 drops taken orally three times daily (TID). For premenstrual syndrome (PMS), the dose ranges from 4-20 mg per day, while for premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), the dose is 20-40 mg per day. The maximum daily dose should not exceed 1800 mg. Chasteberry is used to address a variety of conditions, including acne, benign prostatic hyperplasia, fibrocystic breast disease, impotence, female infertility, lactation issues, menopausal symptoms, menstrual irregularities, premenstrual syndrome (PMS), and progesterone insufficiency. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) published in the BMJ (2001;322:134-137) demonstrated its benefits compared to a placebo. It is considered possibly effective for treating PMS and PMDD. Chasteberry has potential pharmacodynamic interactions with certain medications, particularly antipsychotics. It may reduce the effects of aripiprazole, benperidol, chlorpromazine, clozapine, droperidol, fluphenazine, haloperidol, iloperidone, loxapine (oral and inhaled), olanzapine, paliperidone, perphenazine, pimozide, prochlorperazine, promethazine, quetiapine, risperidone, thioridazine, thiothixene, trifluoperazine, ziprasidone, and zotepine. These interactions are thought to occur due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, but their clinical significance is unknown and remains theoretical. Adverse effects associated with chasteberry include acne, agitation, allergic reactions, alopecia, dry mouth, gastrointestinal upset, headache, intermenstrual bleeding, itching, changes in menstrual flow, nausea, rash, tachycardia, tiredness, and urticaria. It is contraindicated in individuals with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast cancer, endometriosis, ovarian cancer, uterine cancer, and uterine fibroids. It is also not recommended for use during in vitro fertilization. Chasteberry is considered unsafe during pregnancy and lactation. It is classified as unsafe in these contexts due to potential risks. However, in general, it is regarded as acceptable for use in non-pregnant individuals, as controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk.
